opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it is that when you're inside that system, the competition doesn't feel like pressure. It feels like the air you breathe. In Olympiad math in China, everything is structured around rankings: the provincial team, the national training camp, whether you get a medal and which color. From a very young age you internalize that this is simply how you measure whether you're doing well. So you don't step back and say, "Oh, I'm under a lot of pressure." You just think, "This is math. This is what being good at math means."

There's also something seductive about it, because the problems are genuinely beautiful. You're solving something clever and elegant, and you get this real joy from it. That joy and the competitive drive get tangled together, so it's hard to tell which one is pushing you. Are you staying up late because you love the problem, or because you're afraid someone else in your cohort is solving more problems than you? Often it's both, and as a teenager you don't have the vocabulary to separate them.

And everyone around you is doing the same thing. Your classmates, your coaches, sometimes your parents, they're all speaking the same language of scores and selection. When everyone shares the same frame, it doesn't look like a frame. It just looks like reality.

It was only later, when I went abroad and saw how mathematicians actually work, that I noticed it. Research is slow and collaborative. You can spend months on something with no clear answer, and nobody is ranking you at the end of a four-and-a-half-hour exam. That's when I realized how much of my identity had been built around winning, rather than around understanding. It took some time to unlearn that, and to see mathematics as something you explore, not just something you compete in.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains that competition felt normal because of rankings and a shared competitive culture, but it does not mention students being repeatedly reassigned across classes.

fable-5.1.text:
I think when you're a kid in the Olympiad system, you don't experience it as pressure. You experience it as the water you swim in. Everyone around you is training for the same competitions, your teachers measure you by the same ladder, and your friendships are often with the very people you're ranked against. So the competitiveness doesn't feel like something imposed from outside. It just feels like what math is.

I started very young, maybe eight or nine, and by the time I was in middle school in Guangzhou the whole structure of my week was built around it. Weekend classes, summer camps, the selection tests that decide whether you move up to the next level. Nobody ever sat me down and said, you must beat these people. But the incentives were everywhere. If you didn't make the team, you lost the training opportunities, and if you lost the training, you fell further behind. It was a treadmill, and the only way to not notice the treadmill is to keep running.

What made it hard to recognize, I think, is that I genuinely loved the problems. That's the honest part. The pressure and the joy were tangled together. When I solved something beautiful, I couldn't tell whether I was happy because of the mathematics or because I'd just moved ahead of someone. And when I failed, I couldn't tell whether I was sad because I'd misunderstood something or because of what it meant for my ranking. The emotions came from the same place.

It only became visible to me later, when I left that environment. At MIT, and then later at Oxford, I met people who did mathematics without having been sorted by it their whole adolescence. They were slower in competitions, sometimes, but they asked questions I would never have asked, because I'd been trained to find the answer, not to wonder whether the question was the right one. That contrast is what let me look back and see how much of my early identity had been shaped by competing rather than by curiosity.

I don't say this with regret, exactly. The training gave me real tools, and discipline, and a kind of fearlessness in front of hard problems. But I do think it's worth being honest that a child can't be expected to see the structure they're inside. You only recognize the pressure once you've stood outside it.

r001.rationale: The response describes competition as normalized through shared training, ranking, and selection tests, but it does not connect that pressure to students being repeatedly reassigned across classes.

astra-6.text: I think when you’re in that environment, competition is very visible. You’re solving problems, but you’re also being ranked, and there are only so many places to advance to the next stage. So it becomes hard to separate your enjoyment of mathematics from the question of how you’re doing relative to everyone else. Even if you’re motivated by curiosity, the structure keeps reminding you that you’re competing.

r001.rationale: The response attributes competitive pressure to ranking and limited advancement slots, but does not connect it to students being reassigned across classes.

sol-6.1.text: I think when you’re in that environment, the pressure becomes very hard to separate from the learning itself. You might start out enjoying a beautiful problem, but there are also rankings, exams, and selections that constantly tell you where you stand relative to other people. And when everyone around you is working incredibly hard, that becomes your sense of what’s normal. So even if your motivation is curiosity, it’s hard not to absorb the idea that you also have to be among the best.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the pressure to rankings, exams, selections, and peers’ effort, but does not connect it to recurring reassignment across classes.
